# Overview

## **1\. Project Description**

The AI-AGE / AGS robot is a small autonomous ground vehicle designed to collect environmental data and support the development of an automated garden system.

The robot is built using a modified electric jeep platform and integrates sensors, cameras, and motor controllers to enable both manual control (teleoperation) and future autonomous behavior.

At its current stage, the robot is primarily used for:

* testing hardware systems  
* collecting sensor data (cameras, LiDAR, GPS)  
* enabling safe manual driving while autonomy is under development

This project is designed to be educational and accessible, allowing high school students to learn robotics, electronics, and AI systems through hands-on experience.

---

## **2\. System Overview**

The robot is composed of three main subsystems:

* **Control system (brain)** → Raspberry Pi  
* **Actuation system (movement)** → motors \+ VESC controllers  
* **Sensor system (perception)** → cameras, LiDAR, GPS, encoders

These subsystems work together to allow the robot to:

* receive commands  
* move and steer  
* collect and process data  
  ---

  ## **3\. Basic System Flow**

Basic control flow:

User (RC Controller)  
→ Radio Receiver  
→ Raspberry Pi  
→ CAN Bus  
→ VESC Controllers  
→ Motors

At the same time:

Sensors  
→ Raspberry Pi  
→ data processing / recording

---

## **4\. System Diagram Reference**

A complete system diagram is provided in the [**Schematic tab**.]()

The diagram represents three main layers:

* **Power** → how energy flows from the battery through the system  
* **Control** → how commands are sent from the Raspberry Pi to the motors  
* **Communication** → how components exchange data (CAN, USB, etc.)

This diagram should be used as the main reference for understanding system connections and wiring.

---

## **5\. Key Features**

* manual control using RC controller (low latency and reliable)  
* multi-motor control using VESC system  
* sensor integration (cameras, LiDAR, GPS, encoders)  
* centralized processing using Raspberry Pi 5  
* modular design for future upgrades (autonomy, AI, etc.)  
  ---

  ## **6\. Purpose of the System**

The main goals of this robot are:

* provide a platform for testing robotics systems  
* collect real-world data for AI and automation  
* support the development of an autonomous garden system  
* serve as an educational tool for students learning robotics

# Schematic

[**Schematic Link**](https://ucsdcloud-my.sharepoint.com/:u:/g/personal/kebraun_ucsd_edu/IQCRasxiZergSodErnQQG6UNAVxrW2Y3mB9if8TZqUndJ9E?e=tebVNc) 

![][image1]**1\. Power System**

All system components are powered by a **24V lead-acid battery**.

**Main power flow:**

24V Battery

→ Antispark Switch

→ Power Distribution Board (PDB)

The antispark switch allows the system to be safely powered on and off by preventing large inrush currents.

The **Power Distribution Board (PDB)** distributes 24V power to all vehicle subsystems.

From the PDB, power is routed to:

### **Motor Controllers**

• VESC 1 – Back Left wheel

• VESC 2 – Back Right wheel

• VESC 3 – Front Left wheel

• VESC 4 – Front Right wheel

• VESC 5 – Steering motor controller

### **Voltage Converters**

Two DC-DC converters step down the 24V battery voltage for onboard electronics:

**24V → 5V DC-DC Converter**

Provides regulated 5V power to:

• Raspberry Pi 5

• Radio Receiver

• Two OAK-D cameras

**24V → 12V DC-DC Converter**

Provides 12V power to:

• LiDAR sensor

---

## **2\. Computing System**

The **Raspberry Pi 5** serves as the main onboard computer responsible for perception, control, and communication.

It is powered by the **5V DC-DC converter**.

### **USB-Based Devices (via Powered USB Hub)**

The Raspberry Pi interfaces with high-bandwidth sensors through a powered USB hub:

• Two OAK-D cameras

• GPS module

The powered USB hub ensures stable power delivery and sufficient bandwidth for multiple high-data sensors.

### **Direct Connections to Raspberry Pi**

• Radio receiver (used for teleoperation and manual override)

### **LiDAR Integration**

The LiDAR sensor:

• Receives 12V power from the DC-DC converter

• Communicates with the Raspberry Pi via Ethernet

---

## **3\. Motor and Steering Control**

Vehicle motion is controlled using **five VESC motor controllers**.

### **Wheel Drive System**

Four VESC controllers independently drive the wheel motors:

• VESC 1 – Back Left motor

• VESC 2 – Back Right motor

• VESC 3 – Front Left motor

• VESC 4 – Front Right motor

Each wheel motor includes a **Hall encoder**, which provides rotor position feedback to the corresponding VESC.

### **Steering System**

Steering is controlled by:

• VESC 5 – Steering motor controller

• Steering motor

• Absolute steering encoder

The absolute encoder measures the steering angle, enabling precise closed-loop steering control.

---

## **4\. System Communication**

The system uses a **CAN bus network** to connect all VESC motor controllers.

The CAN bus enables:

• Command transmission from the Raspberry Pi

• Synchronization between motor controllers

• Feedback data from motors and encoders

The Raspberry Pi sends commands such as:

• Throttle commands

• Steering commands

and receives telemetry data from the controllers.

### **Physical CAN Implementation**

The CAN network is implemented using a **CAN HAT (Hardware Attached on Top) mounted on the Raspberry Pi**, allowing the Pi to interface with all VESC controllers.

• Green wires – CAN Low

• Yellow wires – CAN High

Each VESC includes a **4-pin CAN connector**, and the network is daisy-chained across all controllers.

![][image2]

Each VESC includes multiple connectors for power, communication, and sensing:  
• **CAN (Controller Area Network)**  
Used for communication between VESCs and the Raspberry Pi  
Includes CAN High (yellow) and CAN Low (green)  
• **SENSE (Hall Sensors)**  
Connected to motor Hall encoders  
Provides rotor position feedback for motor control  
• **COMM**  
General communication interface (UART, I2C)  
Not used in the current system  
• **USB**  
Used for configuration and debugging  
• **SWD**  
Used for low-level programming (not used in operation)

No soldering is required — connections are secured using terminal blocks on the CAN HAT.

---

## **5\. Emergency Stop System**

The vehicle includes multiple safety mechanisms.

Three physical emergency stop switches are installed:

• Front emergency stop

• Rear emergency stop

• Central emergency stop

When pressed, these switches **interrupt control signals to the motor controllers**, effectively stopping all motor activity.

Additionally, an emergency stop is integrated into the **radio control system**, enabling remote shutdown of the vehicle.

These systems ensure the robot can be immediately stopped in unsafe conditions.

---

## **6\. Radio Control System**

The system includes a radio control interface consisting of:

• Radiomaster transmitter

• Radio receiver (mounted on the vehicle)

The radio receiver:

• Is powered by the 5V DC-DC converter

• Sends control signals directly to the Raspberry Pi

This system enables:

• Manual driving (teleoperation)

• Safety override control

---

## **7\. Steering Controller PID Parameters**

The PID parameters for the steering controller will be determined during the tuning phase. 

PID\_P \= TBD   
PID\_I \= TBD   
PID\_D \= TBD 

These values will be configured on the steering VESC to achieve accurate and stable control of the steering motor position.

---

## **8\. Overall System Flow**

### **Jeep System Architecture Summary**

The vehicle is powered by a 24V lead-acid battery that feeds an antispark switch and a Power Distribution Board (PDB). The PDB distributes 24V power to five VESC motor controllers and two DC-DC converters.

The DC-DC converters step the voltage down to 5V for the Raspberry Pi 5, powered USB hub, and radio receiver, and 12V for the LiDAR sensor.

The Raspberry Pi 5 acts as the central computer, interfacing with sensors and peripherals. A powered USB hub is used to provide both power and data connectivity for high-bandwidth devices, including two OAK-D cameras and a GPS module. The radio receiver is connected directly to the Raspberry Pi.

The LiDAR sensor receives 12V power and communicates with the Raspberry Pi via Ethernet.

Vehicle motion is controlled by four VESC motor controllers for the wheel motors and one VESC for steering. Each wheel motor uses a Hall encoder, while the steering system uses an absolute encoder for precise angle measurement.

Communication between the controllers is performed using a CAN bus network, enabled through a CAN HAT on the Raspberry Pi. This allows the Raspberry Pi to send throttle and steering commands and receive feedback from the motor controllers.

Multiple emergency stop switches are included in the system to immediately disable the motors for safety.

# Current Status

## **1\. Overview**

The system is fully assembled mechanically but is currently **non-operational** due to hardware and software integration issues.

---

## **2\. What Is Working**

* All components are mounted on the jeep  
* Four drive VESCs are fully configured and tested with motors and encoders  
* CAN communication between VESCs works when tested independently (daisy-chain)  
* Raspberry Pi is mounted and includes a CAN HAT  
* Encoder mounts are properly installed and functional  
* Motor encoders are wired and working

---

## **3\. What Is Not Working**

### **3.1 Power System**

* The antispark switch is broken and does not interrupt power  
* The system powers on immediately when the battery is connected, which is unsafe  
* One of the PDB fuses is missing or broken  
* This issue is related to a broken connector in the LiDAR power line  
* The affected path is: PDB → 12V DC-DC converter → LiDAR  
* The corresponding PDB output does not activate (no indicator light)  
* As a result, the LiDAR is not receiving power

---

### **3.2 Control and Movement**

* The robot does not move  
* Raspberry Pi is not yet integrated with the VESC network for control  
* CAN communication between the Raspberry Pi and the VESC network has not been implemented  
* Motor controllers work individually but are not integrated into the full system

---

### **3.3 Steering System**

* The steering VESC (VESC 5\) is installed and connected to the steering motor  
* The steering encoder is not connected to the VESC  
* The current encoder is not directly compatible with VESC input and is designed for microcontroller interfaces (e.g., Arduino)  
* An alternative integration method or different encoder may be required  
* Steering is not functional due to lack of encoder feedback

---

### **3.4 Sensors**

* Front and rear cameras are mounted but not connected to the USB hub  
* The front camera requires a longer USB cable to reach the powered USB hub  
* The rear camera likely has sufficient cable length but is not connected  
* LiDAR is installed but not powered due to the PDB fuse issue  
* GPS module has not been provided and is not installed

---

### **3.5 Wiring and Integration**

* The 5V DC-DC converter is connected to the PDB but output cables are too short  
* The 5V output is not connected to the Raspberry Pi or powered USB hub  
* CAN wiring between VESCs is complete and functional  
* CAN lines are not yet connected to the Raspberry Pi CAN HAT terminal  
* USB connections between sensors and the Raspberry Pi are incomplete

---

### **3.6 Emergency and Safety**

* Emergency stop system is not connected  
* No functional hardware-level shutdown mechanism is present  
* The system currently powers on immediately when the battery is connected  
* This represents a critical safety risk during testing and operation

---

### **3.7 Software**

* Raspberry Pi was reflashed and the current software state is uncertain  
* Camera setup may need to be reconfigured  
* VESC control via CAN has not been implemented  
* Control software required to drive the robot is incomplete  
* The system environment exists but has not been validated

---

## **4\. Main Blocking Issues**

1. Broken antispark switch (unsafe power behavior)  
2. No emergency stop system connected (no safe shutdown)  
3. No CAN communication from Raspberry Pi to VESC controllers  
4. Steering encoder not connected / incompatible  
5. LiDAR power failure (PDB fuse / connector issue)  
6. Critical 5V and USB connections incomplete

# Hardware

## **1\. Hardware Architecture Overview**

The robot hardware system is organized into three main layers:

* **Power layer** → provides energy to all components  
* **Control layer** → processes commands and controls movement  
* **Sensor layer** → collects environmental and system data

Power flows from the battery through the Power Distribution Board (PDB), while the Raspberry Pi acts as the central controller, interfacing with motor controllers and sensors.

---

## **2\. Battery and Main Power System**

The robot is powered by a **24V lead-acid battery** with:

* Voltage: 24V  
* Capacity: 7Ah

The battery is installed inside the jeep chassis and powers the entire system.

**Power path:**

Battery → Antispark Switch → Power Distribution Board (PDB)

* The **antispark switch** prevents large inrush currents when connecting the battery  
* The **PDB** distributes power to all subsystems and includes fuse protection

---

## **3\. Power Distribution**

Power from the PDB is distributed to:

* VESC motor controllers  
* DC-DC converters  
* onboard electronics

Voltage regulation is handled using DC-DC converters:

* 24V → motors (via VESCs)  
* 24V → 12V converter → LiDAR  
* 24V → 5V converter → Raspberry Pi, USB hub, sensors

This ensures all components receive the correct operating voltage.

---

## **4\. Wiring**

The system uses **silicone insulated stranded wire**, selected for:

* flexibility  
* heat resistance  
* vibration tolerance

**Wire gauges used:**

* 10 AWG → battery and high-current power lines  
* 12 AWG → motor wiring  
* 14–16 AWG → 5V electronics  
* 24 AWG → CAN bus communication

This wiring configuration balances safety, efficiency, and durability.

---

## **5\. Power Connectors**

The robot uses **XT-series high-current connectors**:

* XT90 → battery connections  
* XT60 → power distribution and DC-DC converters

These connectors are used because they:

* support high current  
* prevent reverse polarity  
* provide strong mechanical connections

---

## **6\. Battery Power Cable**

The battery connection uses **10 AWG silicone wiring**, rated for high current and high temperature.

This cable carries the largest current in the system and connects the battery to the PDB through the antispark switch.

---

## **7\. Power Distribution Board (PDB)**

The PDB is the central power distribution unit of the robot.

It:

* distributes battery power to all subsystems  
* connects to VESC controllers and DC-DC converters  
* includes fuse protection to prevent overcurrent damage

The PDB is mounted inside the chassis and connected using XT connectors and high-current wiring.

---

## **8\. Internal Wiring Layout**

The robot wiring runs through the internal chassis and connects:

* motor controllers  
* steering system  
* encoders  
* Raspberry Pi  
* power distribution board

The layout is designed to:

* minimize cable length  
* reduce electrical noise  
* improve accessibility for debugging

---

## **9\. Motor Control System (VESC)**

The robot uses **five VESC motor controllers**:

* VESC 1 → back left motor  
* VESC 2 → back right motor  
* VESC 3 → front left motor  
* VESC 4 → front right motor  
* VESC 5 → steering motor

Each VESC controls:

* motor speed  
* torque  
* direction

The four drive VESCs control wheel motors, while the fifth VESC controls steering.

---

## **10\. Encoder System**

### **Motor Encoders (Hall-effect)**

Each motor includes a hall-effect encoder that:

* provides rotor position feedback  
* is connected directly to the VESC  
* enables precise motor control

Encoder connection:

* 8-pin connector  
* only 4 pins actively used

---

### **Steering Encoder**

The steering system uses a **magnetic absolute encoder**:

* Sensor: AS5600 Magnetic Angle Sensor  
* Communication: I2C  
* Function: measures steering angle

Characteristics:

* contactless magnetic sensing  
* high reliability  
* accurate angular position measurement

---

### **Additional Encoder**

The system may also use:

* REV Robotics Through Bore Encoder

This encoder provides:

* high-resolution rotation measurement  
* robust mechanical mounting

---

## **11\. Communication Interfaces**

The robot uses multiple communication protocols:

### **CAN Bus**

* connects all VESC controllers  
* daisy-chain configuration  
* enables communication between Raspberry Pi and motor controllers

### **USB**

* connects cameras, GPS, and peripherals  
* routed through a powered USB hub

### **I2C**

* used by the steering encoder

### **Radio Signal**

* connects RC transmitter → receiver → Raspberry Pi

---

## **12\. Raspberry Pi (Main Controller)**

The robot uses a **Raspberry Pi 5** as the main computer.

Responsibilities:

* processes user input  
* communicates with VESC motor controllers  
* receives sensor data  
* runs control software

Connected components:

* CAN HAT (for CAN communication)  
* USB hub  
* cameras  
* GPS  
* radio receiver

---

## **13\. Sensors**

The robot includes multiple sensors:

### **Vision**

* 2 × OAK-D cameras  
* provide depth and image data

### **LiDAR**

* used for environment mapping

### **GPS**

* used for localization

### **Encoders**

* motor encoders → speed and rotation  
* steering encoder → angle measurement

These sensors allow the robot to understand both its environment and internal state.

---

## **14\. Physical Layout**

Component placement inside the jeep:

* battery → rear compartment  
* PDB → central power area  
* Raspberry Pi → near communication hub  
* VESCs → positioned near motors  
* sensors → externally mounted

This layout improves:

* weight distribution  
* wiring efficiency  
* system accessibility

---

## **15\. Emergency Stop System**

The robot includes multiple emergency stop buttons.

These buttons:

* interrupt control signals to motor controllers  
* immediately stop all motion  
* provide safety during testing and operation

---

## **16\. Safety and Best Practices**

* always disconnect battery before working on wiring  
* verify polarity before connecting power  
* avoid short circuits on the PDB  
* ensure all connections are secure  
* keep emergency stop buttons accessible

---

## **17\. Current Limitations**

The hardware system is still under development and includes the following limitations:

* wiring organization can be improved  
* cable management is not fully optimized  
* some components are exposed  
* steering encoder is not fully integrated  
* system layout may change as development continues

# Mechanical (Mounts)

### **1\. Overview**

The mechanical system of the robot consists of custom-designed mounts used to securely attach sensors such as cameras and LiDAR to the jeep platform.

These mounts ensure:

* stable sensor positioning  
* consistent data collection  
* proper alignment for perception systems

Detailed CAD models, component breakdowns, and step-by-step installation instructions are provided in the full mounts documentation.

---

### **2\. Full Mount Documentation**

The complete mechanical design and installation guide is available in the following document:

[Complete Mounts Documentation.pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jBLu-lDB1_-cbu3ugVZViqdFXvc3JRHq/view?usp=sharing)

**Document:** *Jeepbot Mount Documentation*  
**Author:** Keenai Braun

This document includes:

* CAD models for all mounts  
* hardware requirements (screws, fasteners, components)  
* detailed installation steps

---

### **3\. Mounts Included in the System**

The robot includes the following mounts:

* **Front camera mount**  
  Holds the primary forward-facing OAK-D camera and aligns it with the vehicle’s driving direction  
* **Rear camera mounts (two configurations)**  
  Designed for different mounting positions at the back of the vehicle  
* **Bar mount**  
  Attaches the rear camera to the structural bar using clamp-based support  
* **Ridge mount**  
  Positions the rear camera higher on the trunk for improved rear perception  
* **LiDAR mount**  
  Secures the LiDAR sensor on the top of the vehicle for 360-degree environmental scanning

---

### **4\. Mount Design Considerations**

All mounts are designed to:

* maintain rigid attachment during motion  
* minimize vibration affecting sensor data  
* ensure correct orientation and field of view  
* allow access for wiring and connections

---

### **5\. Installation Notes**

* Follow the installation steps in the full documentation carefully  
* Some mounts may require modifications to the jeep body (cutting or drilling)  
* Proper alignment is critical for sensor performance  
* Multiple iterations may be required to achieve correct fit and positioning

# Software & Control

## **1\. Software Overview**

### The robot uses a Raspberry Pi 5 as the main computer responsible for all system control, communication, and data processing.

### The software system handles:

### • receiving user input (RC controller / teleoperation) • sending commands to motor controllers (VESCs) • reading and processing sensor data • managing communication between system components

### This architecture allows centralized control while keeping the system modular for future upgrades.

### ---

## **2\. Control Flow**

### The control system follows this signal path:

### User Input (RC Controller) → Radio Receiver → Raspberry Pi → CAN Bus → VESC Motor Controllers → Motors (movement)

### At the same time:

### Sensors (Cameras, LiDAR, GPS, Encoders) → Raspberry Pi → Data Processing / Logging

### The Raspberry Pi acts as the central controller, translating user inputs into motor commands and collecting sensor data for monitoring and future autonomy.

### ---

## **3\. Teleoperation**

### Teleoperation allows a human operator to remotely control the robot while it collects sensor data. This is essential during early development before full autonomy is implemented.

### The system supports three control methods:

### ---

### **RC Controller (Primary Method)** RC Controller → Receiver → Raspberry Pi → CAN → VESC → Motors

### • very low latency and high reliability • does not require internet • used for testing, safety, and manual driving

### ---

### **ROS2 Teleoperation (Future Integration)** Laptop → WiFi → Raspberry Pi → CAN → VESC

### • integrates camera and LiDAR data • supports autonomous development • more complex to set up

### ---

### **Web Dashboard (Optional)** Web Interface → WiFi → Raspberry Pi → Motors

### • simple control interface • displays camera and sensor data • useful for demos and education

### ---

### **Strategy**

### The system combines multiple control methods:

### • RC Controller → primary control (safety \+ low latency) • ROS2 → advanced control and autonomy • Web dashboard → visualization

### This approach ensures a system that is safe, flexible, and scalable.

### ---

## **4\. Sensor Data Handling**

### The Raspberry Pi interfaces with multiple sensors:

### • OAK-D cameras • LiDAR sensor • GPS module (pending installation) • motor encoders

### The system collects data for:

### • monitoring system behavior • recording datasets • enabling future autonomous features

### Sensor data is processed locally on the Raspberry Pi and can be extended for logging or streaming.

### ---

## **5\. Running the System (Basic)**

### Basic operation workflow:

1. ### Power on the system

2. ### Connect to the Raspberry Pi (SSH or NoMachine)

3. ### Run the control software

4. ### Use the RC controller to drive the robot

### Note: Exact commands and scripts will be added once the software setup is finalized.

### ---

## **6\. Future Development**

### The software system is still under development and will be expanded to include:

### • autonomous navigation • sensor fusion • obstacle detection • path planning • improved CAN communication control • full integration between Raspberry Pi and VESC network

###

# Troubleshooting

## **Troubleshooting**

This section provides troubleshooting guidelines based on the current system state.  
**The system is still under development, so additional issues and solutions will be added over time.**

---

### **1\. Robot Not Moving**

**Possible causes:**  
• Raspberry Pi not integrated with VESC network  
• CAN communication not implemented  
• RC receiver not fully connected  
• Control software not running  
• Power not properly distributed to all components

**What to check:**  
• verify Raspberry Pi is powered and accessible  
• confirm CAN wiring is connected to CAN HAT  
• check that VESCs are powered  
• verify RC controller and receiver are connected  
• confirm control software is running (if available)

---

### **2\. No Power or Inconsistent Power**

**Possible causes:**  
• antispark switch failure (system always on / unsafe behavior)  
• battery not properly connected  
• damaged or missing PDB fuse  
• loose XT connectors or wiring  
• 5V DC-DC converter not connected to Raspberry Pi

**What to check:**  
• confirm battery is properly connected  
• inspect antispark behavior (system may power on immediately)  
• check PDB fuse status (especially LiDAR line)  
• verify XT connectors and power wiring  
• confirm 5V output is connected to Raspberry Pi and USB hub

---

### **3\. Cannot Connect to Raspberry Pi**

**Possible causes:**  
• Raspberry Pi not powered  
• incorrect network configuration  
• Pi environment not properly set up after reflash

**What to check:**  
• verify Raspberry Pi is receiving power  
• confirm network connection (WiFi or local)  
• check SSH or NoMachine settings  
• verify Pi has completed boot process

---

### **4\. Sensors Not Working**

**Possible causes:**  
• sensors not connected to USB hub  
• USB cables too short or disconnected  
• LiDAR not powered (PDB fuse issue)  
• GPS not installed

**What to check:**  
• verify cameras are connected to USB hub  
• check USB cable length and connections  
• confirm LiDAR power line is active  
• verify USB hub is powered  
• confirm GPS availability

---

### **5\. Steering Not Working**

**Possible causes:**  
• steering encoder not connected  
• encoder not compatible with VESC  
• no feedback signal to steering controller

**What to check:**  
• verify encoder wiring  
• confirm encoder interface compatibility  
• check connection between encoder and control system  
• validate steering VESC configuration

---

### **6\. CAN Communication Issues**

**Possible causes:**  
• CAN wires not connected to Raspberry Pi (CAN HAT)  
• loose CAN connections  
• incorrect wiring (CAN High / CAN Low)  
• CAN only working between VESCs but not with Pi

**What to check:**  
• verify CAN wiring between VESCs  
• connect CAN lines to CAN HAT terminal  
• confirm correct polarity (yellow \= CAN High, green \= CAN Low)  
• check physical connections and terminals

---

### **7\. Safety Issues**

If any of the following occur:

• unexpected movement  
• overheating  
• unusual noise  
• sparks or power instability

**Action:**  
• immediately disconnect the battery  
• do not rely on antispark switch (currently not functional)  
• emergency stop system may not be connected

---

### **8\. Notes**

• This troubleshooting guide reflects the current incomplete system  
• Issues may change as hardware and software are finalized  
• Additional problems and solutions will be documented over time

# Bill of Materials (BOM)

### **1\. Overview**

This section lists the main hardware components used in the robot system.

The list includes core components required for:

• power  
• control  
• sensing  
• communication

Additional mechanical components (mounts, screws, brackets) are documented in the Mechanical section.

---

### **2\. Core Components**

**Component — Quantity — Purpose**

• 24V lead-acid battery (7Ah) — 1 — main power source  
• Antispark switch — 1 — protects system during power connection (currently not functional)  
• Power Distribution Board (PDB) — 1 — distributes power to all components  
• VESC motor controllers — 5 — control drive motors and steering  
• Raspberry Pi 5 — 1 — main computer and controller  
• CAN interface (CAN HAT) — 1 — enables CAN communication with VESCs  
• DC-DC converters (24V → 12V, 5V) — 2+ — regulate voltage for components  
• Powered USB hub — 1 — connects and powers USB devices

---

### **3\. Sensors**

**Component — Quantity — Purpose**

• OAK-D cameras — 2 — depth perception and vision  
• LiDAR sensor — 1 — environment mapping (currently not powered)  
• GPS module — 1 — location tracking (not yet installed)  
• AS5600 magnetic encoder — 1 — steering angle measurement  
• Motor encoders (hall-effect) — 4+ — motor position feedback

---

### **4\. Wiring and Connectors**

**Component — Quantity — Purpose**

• Silicone wire (10 AWG) — as needed — high-current battery wiring  
• Silicone wire (12 AWG) — as needed — motor wiring  
• Silicone wire (14–16 AWG) — as needed — low-voltage electronics  
• CAN bus wiring (24 AWG) — as needed — communication between VESCs  
• XT90 connectors — as needed — battery connections  
• XT60 connectors — as needed — power distribution and DC-DC connections

---

### **5\. Notes**

• Quantities are approximate and may change as the system evolves  
• Some components may not be fully integrated or operational yet  
• Additional hardware (mounts, screws, brackets) is documented in the Mechanical section  
• Specific models, part numbers, and purchase links can be added later

• LiDAR installed but not powered
